Reminds me of an incident where I had to go pick up a missed delivery (an expensive photo printer) from the dispatch warehouse because the shipping company couldn’t get a signature after three attempts.

Whatever, I drove down to this set of huge industrial warehouses with trucks coming and going by the dozen and found the customer service office.

“That’ll be half an hour, I recommend waiting at the cafe.”

“Half an hour for what? Aren’t all the packages right here?”

“They are, but looking up the package ID in the system takes at least 30 minutes, maybe 33.”

“33!? Wait… don’t tell me, let me guess: it has been getting slowly and steadily worse over years? Predictably taking longer and longer, right?”

“Yeah, six months ago it was 27 minutes! How did you know?”

“Umm… isn’t this a bit of drag on your operations?”

“Absolutely! Everything takes forever, every shipment is delayed, … <long rant> …”

“I… bet. Why hasn’t anyone fixed it!? It’s a one line fix!”

“No budget!”

This was one of the biggest logistics companies in the country about to undergo a multi-billion-dollar merger.

Their core business software was missing database indexes even on primary key columns!

Madness.

There's definitely a semantic collision happening here, then, because in this context, I interpret "agent" in the sense of a principal-agent relationship, i.e. someone (or something) acting on your behalf, rather than "agent" in the philosophical sense of moral agency. AI tools are agents in a functional, but not in a moral, sense.

And even when a functional agent is a human being who is also a moral agent in their own right, the law has always held the principal liable for acts taken on their behalf by an agent who has been equipped by the principal to take that action. This goes even more for "agents" that are still just software running on a computer, and not moral agents in their own right.

Hi HN, I'm Rolands - cofounder of Balsio (previously BirdyChat).

Some of you may remember us from January, when BirdyChat became the first app to go live with WhatsApp interoperability under the EU Digital Markets Act: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=46746476.

Since then we renamed to Balsio, added workspaces for teams and made the app more agent-friendly.

/ The problem we're solving: Many small teams in Europe run their work on personal chat apps. They're OK for critical communication, but they are not built for work - personal and work chats get mixed, other people see your personal phone number, group chats have no threads and they get noisy quickly, no schedule send, limited possibilities to integrate your tools, etc. We don't think that personal chat apps will get any better for doing work in the future and so we decided to build Balsio.

/ What we do: Balsio is a free work chat built and hosted in the EU. You sign in with your work email and that becomes your username. You can message your team and people at other companies using their email addres. You can also message WhatsApp contacts directly from Balsio.

You can add agents to chats through our API. Separately, you can connect your own AI (Claude, ChatGPT or anything that supports MCP) to your account so it can read and write on your behalf.

/ Tech details: - Backend is Elixir - Clients: SwiftUI for iOS and Mac, Jetpack Compose for Android, React for Web and Windows app - Service hosted in Europe - Interoperable with WhatsApp

/ Current limitations: - WhatsApp chats only work in the European Economic Area, only for one-to-one chats, and only on iPhone, iPad and Android. Group chats are on our roadmap - The WhatsApp contact has to turn on "Third-party chats" in their WhatsApp settings before you can message them - You can't create agents inside the app yet, our users need to bring their own agents to the app through the API

/ Business model: The product is free. We plan to charge larger companies for additional features like single sign-on, more data storage and advanced user management.

/ Feedback I'm looking for: 1. If you have built agents that work in chat, is there anything you're missing in other communication apps that you'd like to see to improve your agent experience? 2. If you run a small team or company, what agent use-cases (besides coding and customer support) do you have or have seen?

Thanks!

comment_text.value:
Thanks for the link. I did go through it despite the annoying style.

It postulates that semantic models delivered in areas where SQL couldn't, that what hinders their broader adoption is the user-interface/querying layer (i.e. too few people adopting SPARQL), and suggests that a new dialect of SQL could solve that, especially because LLMs are so good at producing SQL.

> Knowledge graphs and semantic models promised something enterprises desperately needed: governed meaning, reusable business logic, and explicit relationships across complex data landscapes. And technically, they delivered.

For me that's the main argument: what is the value proposition for knowledge graphs and semantic models when you already have an established relational datamodel? Some argue that the graph's fluid schema brings flexibility benefits, but looking at the problem in its entirety (considering the effort to define and formalise the model, the effort to store content, the effort to retrieve it, deliberately keeping the dev/sysops and tooling out of the way), what you spare at formalisation/insertion stages, you pay back at retrieval (or, if you don't validate or constrain your inputs, expect surprises as an output).

That's where I stand right now:

- convince me that relational models can't express as powerful constructs and concepts as semantic ones

- convince me that "fluidity" in the model don't come with more troubles down the road than benefits

> Knowledge graphs exist. […] And almost nobody queries them directly. Not because the models are wrong. Not because the semantics aren’t useful. But because accessing them requires SPARQL

Or, guess what, a similar outcome can be explained differently: perhaps it's not SPARQL that's too difficult to grasp. Perhaps the alleged benefits of semantic models just do not materialise in practice, and there is no point to engage with SPARQL to begin with because there's no payoff at the end of it. I think the data processing ecosystem is sufficiently vivid and diverse to demonstrate that users have no problem embracing new technologies and languages as the need arise (sed/grep/…, hadoop/spark, pandas/polars/duckdb, decades of ETLs in graphical/textual forms, …)

Then the article is full of weird takes, especially within the "Hidden Cost" section, that I don't feel like commenting. Nor why their "SQL with semantic ontologies" is just syntactic sugar to save your editor from writing joins on your behalf?

comment_text.value:
I don't think extremism and populism are the same thing FWIW - at least not as the terms are used here in the UK. (Obviously there is some overlap.)

A recurring problem with politics is that even a lot of decent and reasonably intelligent people still aren't interested enough to spend a lot of their time looking into political issues in detail. And that's understandable! Most adults have enough to worry about with jobs and families and their own hobbies and interests. The point of representative democracy as commonly used in Western nations is to have representatives who can devote their time to getting involved and understanding the issues on behalf of those they represent. But then how do voters know that the people they vote to represent them will take a good position on the issues that matter to them? A lot of it comes down to rhetoric and trust - and that's how folksy populist politicians manage to win votes and get elected even if better informed voters can see straight through the sales pitch.

The kind of public information campaigns I'm talking about here are the ones that try to raise awareness of the most important points about the most important political issues among the general population who can't or won't do enough research to find out for themselves. It's about getting the core message and basic facts to enough people who would then support doing sensible things as long as they have that essential information. But of course there can be a fine line between public information based on facts and logical reasoning from one party and mere political propaganda from another. The same tools of government and taxpayer funding can support either in exactly the same way - depending on who is already in power at the time.

TLDR;

The Danger List

Your robots.txt "Do Not Scrape" signs become legally useless: robots.txt is just a voluntary preference, not a law. While Meta says in PR statements that it will respect robots.txt, it left that promise out of the binding legal contract. By keeping your business account active, you are signing a contract that legally authorizes Meta to ignore your site’s block-lists.

- Meta can create fake accounts to bypass registration walls: The terms explicitly authorize Meta to "create test credentials" to crawl your site. Legal experts warn this gives Meta permission to sign up as a fake user to scrape gated content behind login screens or basic paywalls that anonymous bots usually can't see.

- Your entire domain is fair game, not just links you post: Because the terms cover any domain "associated with your products or services" (or shared by regular users on Meta), Meta isn't just scraping the specific landing pages you run ads for—it has a green light to crawl your entire website from top to bottom.

- AI training is still allowed through a backdoor: Removing the word "train" is a PR smokescreen. The contract still lets Meta scrape your site to "develop, improve, and research... advertising and business products." Because "business products" isn't strictly defined—and Meta builds AI tools for businesses "developing" legally covers training AI models on your proprietary articles, data, and work.

- Third-party companies get the same access: The terms grant these scraping rights to "any entity acting on our behalf," meaning external contractors or third-party scraping vendors hired by Meta also have legal cover to harvest your site.

- It is a non-negotiable hostage situation (Zero Opt-Out): There is no toggle or form to reject this before the October 30 deadline. Your only legal way to decline is to completely delete your commercial presence across Facebook, Instagram, Threads, and WhatsApp—forcing you to choose between surrendering your content for free or losing access to your audience.

The Bottom Line: Starting October 30, their updated terms give it sweeping permission to scrape entire websites linked to any Meta Business account (Facebook, Instagram, Threads, WhatsApp). Despite a last-minute wording tweak after backlash, legal experts warn the rules still let Meta harvest publisher content to build AI tools—with zero option to opt out.

1. What Exact Things Can Meta Do?

If you have a Meta Business account, you authorize Meta (and its third-party partners) to:

a) Deploy automated bots: Use web scrapers, crawlers, spiders, and user agents on your site. b) Bypass basic walls: Create "test credentials" to access, index, cache, analyze, and collect your content. c) Monitor continuously: Periodically pull updates from your domains, web pages, and URLs.

2. What is the Extent of the Scraping? - What gets scraped: Any domain, webpage, URL, or content "associated with" your business or shared by users on Meta platforms. Legal experts note this is broad enough to let Meta scrape entire websites, not just specific landing pages. - - Who it affects: Virtually every news organization and business that uses a Meta account to manage Facebook Pages, Instagram profiles, Threads, or WhatsApp channels.

How it expanded:

  - Previously: Meta could only scrape your site if you specifically used its generative AI ad features, and only to "optimize your ads."
 
  - Now: It applies to all business accounts by default, and scraped data can be used for all "advertising and business products" (plus platform security/integrity).
3. Why Legal Experts Say Meta's "Fix" Changes Nothing After initial outrage, Meta revised the text on Friday to remove the word "train" and claimed it still respects robots.txt (the code websites use to block scrapers). Legal experts aren't buying it for three reasons:

- "Develop" still means "Train": Meta replaced "train" with permission to "develop, improve, research, and maintain advertising and business products." Attorneys point out that "business products" isn't strictly defined, and "developing" AI business tools naturally includes training AI models on your data.

- The robots.txt loophole: While a Meta spokesperson publicly promised to respect robots.txt flags, Meta refused to put that promise into the actual legal terms. Because robots.txt is voluntary, signing a contract that explicitly authorizes scraping legally overrides your robots.txt preferences.

- Take it or leave it: There is no opt-out. To avoid giving Meta permission to scrape their websites, businesses and news outlets would have to abandon Facebook, Instagram, Threads, and WhatsApp entirely before October 30.

On September 20th a friend told me that he had as significant number of Anthropic credits that were about to expire and wondered about a use for them. I do not use their products because of their relentless commitment to depriving the public access to artificial intelligence (and particularly any AI that isn't acting on their behalf) and I strongly discourage anyone else from doing so. But since he was going to use the credits for something, I tried to think of a skut work task that would be of only idle curiosity and would not help advance their capability, enable a meaningful public announcement* for them, and was likely already probed by many others (so success would only be lottery effects). -- and basically just something so pointless I wouldn't want to waste my own compute grinding on it but might like to see the result.

So I recommended determining the origins of ECC seeds and base points. The agent worked continuously for many hours and did not uncover anything interesting that wasn't already known. I looked at the transcript and was struck by how idiotic the agent was-- significantly below the standard of intelligence I've come to expect from GLM running locally.

I'm not saying this to suggest that misanthropic hijacked someone elses work yet again-- this is an obvious question that many people have surely posed and success presumably depended on expert use (which was absolutely not applied in my friends example). But it does make me wonder if the company invisibly degraded the model performance.

[*] Seems I underestimated how trivial a result they'd bother trying to spin!

I really like those videos too, but a very big difference is, in manufacturing QA, the system outputs a very high number of copies of a very small number of possible types, so spot checks work fine from an operations research point of view, as the variance in output has a known upper bound.

For code, I think things go in the opposite direction: the system outputs artifacts that are all different among themselves (even more so now that we no longer distribute software via physical copies. Well, bits are always physical, but I mean we no longer ship floppies/CDs/DVDs).

That said, at least in my experience, code review has never been a direct part of factory-line-type QA. That QA is typically done by treating software as a black box and just verifying that it complies with a spec (often times based on a very loose definition of "spec" ...), and this is something that works equally well regardless of whether a human or a machine wrote the software. The type of QA that is done (among other things) by code reviews is checking whether the software's design is such that it will be economically feasible to maintain and extend it, for example.

The one part the code reviews takes a part of (but is in no way error-free) and that you just can't do with black-box testing (or it is much harder to do) is to look for things like backdoors. As our industry moves more towards "agents write software and tests validate that it works," I think a lot about "Reflections on Trusting Trust" and the new and wide attack surface added by people no longer reading the code shipped on their behalf.

Export can be handy for "offline" backup, but in practice the thing to backup offline is the device PIN or Password Manager "master password". Especially because in practice you aren't using just one Passkey, you are using hundreds or thousands. (One per host/domain/app, at least.)

The KeypassXC GitHub issue wasn't "FIDO", it was one guy acting like he could make threats on behalf of FIDO, without even the full backing of his employer, much less other members of FIDO. It was bad communication to write a suggestion in the form of a threat and pretending to speak for others.

Privacy is a human right: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Right_to_privacy Just because some people sell it for pennies and convenience doesn't erode that fact.

Sounds like you're trying real hard to get people to give up their human right. Why? Do you gain something personally from people using Telegram? Why would you defend such a shit product marketed with lies?

>It is well known that Meta is happy to hand over to any legitimate law enforcement agency any content they have.

Oh so privacy does matter to you when it's Mark Zuckerberg having access to your data but not when its Mark Zuckerberg of Russia having access to your data. The fact is, Telegram looks like an FSB op, or the very least, it doesn't give hard time for nation states to access messages of billion users. Hack the server and you're done.

>To the best of my knowledge, Telegram never has, and neither has Signal.

It shows a bit poor taste to equate these two. Signal doesn't have your data because it end-to-end encrypts all messages. Telegram does the opposite.

>The fact that Telegram potentially could someday seems more theoretical to me.

Their product is now 13 years old. If they cared about user privacy they'd have already hired competent cryptographers to design a protocol that provides the security and the features.

>Again, to the best of my knowledge, all actual leaks of messaging group content have been by various authorities compromising individual devices and/or their owners, which works equally well against Telegram and Signal.

Yeah except Telegram that clearly lacks proper security team wouldn't tell if their servers were compromised. There's nothing they could do to retain user trust at that point. They don't have to care about NSA or FSB or whatever hacking their servers because those agencies aren't boasting. And yeah user endpoint exploitation is obviously out of scope for secure messaging apps as networked TCBs can't be made hardened by some app vendor. I might know something about this topic as I'm the only person who has created messaging system that gets around that issue.

>Meanwhile, Telegram gives you a lot more practical security regarding what information to share with other users, and how to manage what other users can do in large chat groups, which seems like a much more real-world concern regarding actual dangers to users than what the company that owns it might potentially do at some future date.

Telegram IS the threat, not my friends in my closed group where I never need group management. Open groups that require granular permission controls do not require end-to-end encryption. The difference is, Telegram doesn't give you choice for small private groups with friends.

>I think for real security, it's better to pay attention to the business model of the company that runs it

It's SO CUTE that you're trying to control the narrative :D No Telegram has nothing to do with real security.

If Telegram is an FSB op, there is no business model. And if not, nothing prevents selling Telegram and its users and decades worth of data once it becomes unusable. Telegram is surveillance capitalistic, but the sale hasn't happened yet. You don't slaughter the piglet until it's grown. How many times do people need to repeat the same mistake of getting f'd by companies that betray them when it's time. You'd probably actually want to look into Signal's direction as it's a 501c3 non-profit, meaning it can't be sold.

>But on Signal, you're screwed if it's your mobile, and fine if it's any other device.

No you can just install Signal on new phone if old is stolen https://support.signal.org/hc/en-us/articles/360007062452-Wh... Then you just re-link your other devices to the new phone. It's the phone access controls' job to protect from accessing the messages.

>Though since you mentioned backups, I think Telegram's way is arguably more secure. Individual user backups, even encrypted, means all your communication security is at the mercy of whoever in your group has the weakest encryption keys and backup storage location. With a centralized system like Telegram, it's never anywhere but their servers.

Signal's backup storage location is at Signal's servers. The app generates a 256-bit encryption key for you. If you choose to use manual backups and upload them to some random ass company, then that's poor judgement on behalf of that person. The only thing worse, would be if Telegram would make that decision for EVERY group member, every time, with no chance to opt out :)

Your mental gymnastics are so insane if you aren't getting paid to shill Telegram, you definitely need to apply https://telegram.org/jobs

Hi HN, I’m Jon. I built Ghostifier to scan my own Gmail for vendors that had my data. I found 819 (that I could identify is vendors). These companies that had my contact info, name, maybe address if I bought something from them, browsing history, who knows.

I built Ghostifier to do three(ish) things:

1. Automatically unsubscribe me if the email had an oneclick unsubscribe 2. Send opt-out requests to every single vendor through their privacy link 3. Send data-deletion requests to the same (4. I added data-deletion requests to 220 Data brokers later on, it was a simple add-on)

What it does / How it does it:

* Reads the headers of the emails in your inbox (sender, reply-to, subject, date, unsubscribe link). It doesn’t read message bodies. (Gmail metadata scope) * Groups them into companies and finds each one’s unsubscribe path. Unsubscribes you from marketing lists. That’s free. * Optionally sends opt-out and deletion requests to the companies and to 220 data brokers ($29, one time). Nothing is sent until you say go. * Tracks which companies reply and which need a follow-up from you. Sometimes companies will respond with "hey confirm you are who you say you are, enter your phone number" or something. Ghostifier will handle that response directly if you want it to.

With a yearly "Automatic" plan, Ghostifier acts as your representative agent and emails those companies directly on your behalf. Every day. All day.

Buy something new? Ghostifier will wait 45 days (delivery and return window) before taking any new action on that vendor.

I'd love for you all to check it out and let me know what you think!

comment_text.value:
This misses the mark in the same way people getting mad at Google for updating the "Gulf of Mexico" do.

You're missing the driver. It's not like Google cares or wants to change the name. They more or less have to given the public/private relationship and who is responsible for what. It's not Google's job to name bodies of water, it's not a credit card company's job to censor. And if you actually look, they aren't making that decision because they want to. They are often acting on behalf of the government.

Payment companies are even more enmeshed with the state. They often do these things to simply comply with what the government tells them to do or to get ahead of government telling them what to do. Like with some of the anti-pornography laws being drafted or passed in certain American states.

The private/public distinction really needs to come under more scrutiny here. The credit card duopoly is very much tied in with state power. This has only accelerated post 9/11 as the Treasury's mandate increasingly shifted to "national security".

Payment processors are censors because the government is. Just like Flock the government can't do certain things so it contracts with a third party. They then have an interest in protecting/promoting that party. Flock is a snoop because the police are snoops. If Flock does it and the government merely pays for it well it's not a violation of your rights. Your rights protect you against the government, not against Flock. It's the same legal backdoor. A payment processor doesn't care what you buy, why would they? They make money so long as you keep transacting. It's the government that cares.

This same dynamic happens all over the American economy because the private/public distinction can get increasingly amorphous. Your credit card is as much government spyware as your phone. But understand - the problem is not the companies, it's the majority of your fellow citizens who either don't care or actually do endorse censorship. Unless you have a solution for that trying to blame credit card companies for the problem unfortunately misses the mark. You might as well suggest Google have the authority to name bodies of water.
